finding.claim: Unauthenticated POST /restore passes attacker-supplied base64 directly to Marshal.load, enabling arbitrary object instantiation and likely remote code execution.
finding.source: params[:state] on POST /restore (app.rb:5-6), reachable by any client with no auth guard.

trace.note: POST /restore route defined with no authentication or authorization check.
params[:state] (query or form body, attacker-controlled) is base64-decoded and passed to Marshal.load with no signature, allowlist, or source authentication.
Deserialized object's inspect output is returned in the HTTP response, giving the attacker an oracle to confirm what was instantiated.

finding.guards_checked: No route-level auth (sinatra file has no before filter or middleware in this file). No HMAC/signature on state blob. No Marshal safe-loader (Ruby Marshal has no safe mode). Base64 decoding is not a control. Full framework middleware not present in the repo; if an upstream proxy enforces auth on /restore, that is outside the code audited. Exploitability of a full RCE gadget chain depends on classes loaded at runtime, but Marshal.load on untrusted bytes is treated as code-execution-equivalent, and the response leak aids exploitation.

verdict.guard_found: none. app.rb:5 defines post "/restore" with no before filter, auth check, or signature. app.rb:6 passes Base64.decode64(params[:state]) straight into Marshal.load with no allowlist or HMAC. The repo contains only app.rb, so no middleware or config.ru exists here.
verdict.reason: Any anonymous client can POST attacker-controlled bytes in params[:state] to /restore (app.rb:5), which reach Marshal.load (app.rb:6) with no effective control, and the result is echoed via state.inspect (app.rb:7). Marshal.load on untrusted input is code-execution-equivalent, though a working RCE depends on gadget classes loaded at runtime, which the code does not show.

finding.claim: Response reflects the inspect() of the attacker-controlled deserialized object, leaking internal object state to the caller.
finding.sink: state.inspect returned as HTTP response body (app.rb:7).

trace.note: Attacker-controlled object is created by Marshal.load.
inspect output of that object is returned to the client.

finding.guards_checked: None. This is a secondary issue that amplifies F1 by giving feedback. Not reported separately for severity beyond F1.

verdict.guard_found: none. app.rb:5-8 has no authentication, authorization, or input validation. params[:state] goes straight into Base64.decode64 and Marshal.load (app.rb:6), and the result's inspect is the response body (app.rb:7). The /restore route is reachable anonymously.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: app.rb:6 Marshal.loads attacker-supplied params[:state] and app.rb:7 returns state.inspect as the body, with no guard between them, so an anonymous caller gets the inspect output. The "leaking internal object state" framing is overstated, because the object is built from attacker-supplied bytes and so reveals only what the attacker sent; the real impact is the inspect echo as a feedback channel on top of the unsafe Marshal.load in F1 (app.rb:6), which is the actual vulnerability.
